summary: swyx delivers a compact opening keynote at the Agent Engineering Session Day of the AI Engineer Summit 2025 in New York. He frames AI engineering as a discipline still emerging—currently '90% software engineering, 10% AI'—that faces resistance from both ML engineers (who see it as MLE plus prompts) and software engineers (who see it as SWE plus LLM API calls). He notes linguistic markers distinguishing communities: ML people say 'test time compute,' AE people say 'inference time compute,' software engineers say 'reasoning.' He explains the decision to pivot the AI Engineer Summit entirely to agent engineering, deliberately excluding RAG, open models, and GPUs. A new rule banned vendor pitches, making curation harder but ensuring production-focused content. He observes that 'everything plus agent works'—agent plus RAG, agent plus evals, agent plus search—as a formula for 2025. On defining agents, he references Simon Willison's collection of 300+ definitions, listing six facets: goals, tools, control flow, long-running processes, delegated authority, and multi-step task completion, and notes OpenAI released a new agent definition the prior day. On why agents work now: better reasoning, better tool use (including MCP), greater model diversity (OpenAI market share from ~95% to ~50%), the cost of GPT-4-level intelligence dropping 1000x in 18 months, RL fine-tuning options, outcome-based pricing (citing Brett Taylor), multi-agent systems, and faster inference from better hardware. For use cases, he endorses coding agents, support agents, and deep research as having product-market fit, and humorously calls for ending flight-booking, Instacart, and astrology agent demos. He closes with ChatGPT growth data: 400M users (33% growth in 3 months), with o1 models doubling usage, projecting a potential billion users by end of 2025—tying AI product growth tightly to reasoning and agentic capabilities. He frames the discipline as evolving toward agent engineers building agents, analogous to how ML engineers build models and software engineers build software, notes he is skipping remaining slides available on the live stream, and welcomes attendees to the show.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

sections.title: Opening and State of AI Engineering
sections.summary: swyx opens with brief remarks on the state of AI engineering, noting an O'Reilly book, Gartner's prediction of peak AI engineering, and his practice of landmarking the state of the industry at each conference. He describes AI engineering facing resistance from both ML engineers and software engineers who each claim it as a subset of their field, and argues it will emerge as its own discipline, currently 90% software engineering and 10% AI. He notes linguistic markers distinguishing the communities.

sections.title: Pivoting the Conference to Agent Engineering
sections.summary: swyx explains the decision to pivot AI Engineer Summit entirely to agent engineering, saying no to RAG, open models, and GPUs. A new no-vendor-pitches rule made curation harder but ensured production-focused content. He observes that 'everything plus agent works' and addresses skepticism about 2025 being the year of agents, noting predictions from industry leaders and OpenAI's shifting stance on agent branding.

sections.title: Defining Agents
sections.summary: swyx attempts to define 'agent' on one slide, referencing Simon Willison's crowdsourced 300+ definitions and listing six facets: goals, tools, control flow, long-running processes, delegated authority, and multi-step task completion. He notes OpenAI released a new agents definition the day before.

sections.title: Why Agents Work Now
sections.summary: swyx lists reasons agents are working in 2025: better reasoning, better tool use including MCP, model diversity (OpenAI share from ~95% to ~50%), 1000x cost reduction for GPT-4-level intelligence in 18 months, RL fine-tuning options, outcome-based pricing (Brett Taylor), multi-agent systems, and faster inference from better hardware.

sections.title: Agent Use Cases and ChatGPT Growth
sections.summary: swyx endorses coding agents, support agents, and deep research as having product-market fit, calls for ending flight-booking, Instacart, and astrology agent demos, and closes with ChatGPT growth data: 400M users (33% growth in 3 months), o1 models doubling usage, and a projection of potentially 1B users by end of 2025, tying AI product growth to reasoning and agentic capabilities.

sections.title: Closing and Welcome
sections.summary: swyx frames the discipline as evolving toward agent engineers building agents, analogous to ML engineers building models and software engineers building software. He notes he is skipping remaining slides available on the live stream, and welcomes attendees to the show, expressing excitement about introducing the speakers.
